intro.en: Nutritional history taking, daily calorie and protein calculations, food composition reference values, and infant feeding rules.

title.en: Paediatric calorie requirements and Holliday-Segar formula

items.summary: Estimation of daily paediatric energy requirements using rapid bedside age-based heuristics and the weight-based Holliday-Segar method.

blocks.title: Rapid bedside clinical calculation
bullets: Infants up to 1 year of age: baseline requirement of 100 cal per kilogram body weight per day.
Children older than 1 year: calculate as 1000 cal baseline plus 100 cal for each additional year of age.
Worked clinical example: for an 8-year-old child, requirement is calculated as 1000 + 700 = 1700 cal per day.

blocks.title: Holliday and Segar weight-tiered formula
bullets: First 10 kilograms of body weight: allocate 100 cal per kilogram per day (100 x 10 = 1000 cal).
Next 11 to 20 kilograms of body weight: add 50 cal per kilogram per day for weight above 10 kg (50 x 10 = 500 cal).
Body weight exceeding 20 kilograms: add 20 cal per kilogram per day for weight above 20 kg.
Worked example for an 8-year-old child weighing 24 kilograms: 1000 cal (first 10 kg) + 500 cal (11 to 20 kg) + 80 cal (20 x 4) = 1580 cal per day.

blocks.title: Clinical utility in disease states
bullets: Serves as the foundation for prescribing intravenous maintenance fluids and enteral nutrition.
Requirements increase during fever, severe burns, sepsis, or catch-up growth in malnutrition.
Requirements may be restricted in congestive heart failure, renal failure, or mechanical ventilation.

viva.q: How do you quickly estimate expected daily calories at the bedside for a child older than 1 year?
viva.a: Prescribe 1000 cal for the first year, then add 100 cal for each additional year of age. For instance, an 8-year-old requires 1000 plus 700, yielding 1700 cal per day.

viva.q: Explain the Holliday-Segar method for calculating daily caloric needs by body weight tiers.
viva.a: Allocate 100 cal per kg for the first 10 kg, 50 cal per kg for 11 to 20 kg, and 20 cal per kg for each kilogram above 20 kg.

title.en: Paediatric protein requirements by age group

items.summary: Recommended daily dietary protein allowances across infancy, childhood, and adolescence, alongside principles for correcting protein deficit.

blocks.title: Age-stratified daily protein requirements
bullets: Infants under 1 year of age: require 2 gm of protein per kilogram body weight per day.
Children aged 1 to 9 years: require 1.5 gm of protein per kilogram body weight per day.
Older children above 9 years of age: require 1.2 gm of protein per kilogram body weight per day.

blocks.title: Biological value and clinical considerations
bullets: Protein quality depends on amino acid composition and net protein utilisation; animal proteins and soy provide high biological value.
Cereal and pulse combinations achieve amino acid complementarity in vegetarian diets.
Children recovering from protein-energy malnutrition require increased protein for tissue catch-up growth.
Adequate non-protein calories from carbohydrates and fats must be provided to spare dietary protein for somatic synthesis.

viva.q: What are the daily dietary protein requirements for infants compared to children aged 1 to 9 years?
viva.a: Infants under one year require 2 gm per kilogram per day, whereas children aged 1 to 9 years require 1.5 gm per kilogram per day.

viva.q: Why must adequate non-protein calories accompany protein supplementation during nutritional recovery?
viva.a: If non-protein calories from carbohydrates and fats are insufficient, dietary amino acids will be oxidised for energy production via gluconeogenesis rather than utilized for tissue building and growth.

image.brief: Staircase graph showing daily protein requirement declining from 2 gm/kg/day in infancy to 1.5 gm/kg/day in young children and 1.2 gm/kg/day in older children.

items.summary: Standard reference table providing caloric and protein content per designated portion size for common Indian staple foods, dairy, snacks, and animal products.

blocks.title: Nutritive values of common foods table
Practical clinical notes on food values
bullets: Milk provides 67 cal and 3 gm protein per 100 ml, while formula milk yields 20 cal and 0.5 gm protein per 30 ml.
One whole egg yields 60 cal and provides 6 gm of complete reference protein.
Meats provide concentrated protein averaging 20 to 25 gm per 100 gm portion.
Fats like ghee and butter contribute dense energy at 36 cal per teaspoon without protein.

viva.q: What is the calorie and protein content of 100 ml of cow's milk?
viva.a: Cow's milk provides 67 cal of energy and 3 gm of protein per 100 ml.

viva.q: How many calories and grams of protein does one egg contribute?
viva.a: One egg provides approximately 60 cal of energy and 6 gm of complete protein.

unsure: The source lists 1 puri as 35 cal and 1 gm protein, whereas 1 chappati is listed as 70 cal and 2 gm protein. Deep-fried puris generally provide higher calories than dry chappatis; the source figure of 35 cal is retained verbatim as an exam fact.
Cooked dal is listed as 10 cal and 1 gm protein per 50 ml big spoon, which reflects a highly diluted home-prepared soup rather than thick lentil curry.

title.en: Dietary rules of thumb, reference measures, and presentation syntax

items.summary: Practical rules for estimating macronutrients in staples, essential fatty and amino acids, standardized household volume measures, and presentation syntax for infant feeds.

blocks.title: Macronutrient rules of thumb for raw food groups
bullets: Uncooked cereals (per 100 gm): rice and ragi provide 350 cal and 7 gm protein; wheat and maize provide 350 cal and 11 gm protein.
Uncooked pulses (per 100 gm): provide approximately 350 cal and 20 gm protein, except soybean which yields 450 cal and 43 gm protein.
Green leafy vegetables: contain negligible calories and proteins.
Fruits: yield approximately 50 cal per fruit with negligible protein, except banana (100 cal) and jackfruit.
Meats (fish, chicken, mutton, beef per 100 gm): provide approximately 250 cal and 20-25 gm protein.
Rice cooking expansion: cooked rice triples in weight compared to raw grain weight.

blocks.title: Essential nutrients and physiological fuel values
bullets: Essential fatty acids: linoleic acid, linolenic acid, and arachidonic acid.
Essential amino acids mnemonic MAT HILL PVT: methionine, arginine, threonine, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, phenylalanine, valine, and tryptophan.
Physiological energy yield: dietary fat produces 9 kcal/gram; protein produces 4 kcal/gram; carbohydrate produces 4 kcal/gram.

blocks.title: Household measures and presentation syntax
bullets: Standard kitchen measures: teaspoon equals 5 ml; tablespoon equals 15 ml; standard katori or cup equals 150 ml; drinking glass equals 250 ml.
Presentation formula for breastfed infants: state that child is consuming specified calories and grams of protein from complementary foods, alongside breastfeeding a specified number of times daily.

viva.q: What are the physiological fuel values per gram for carbohydrates, proteins, and fats?
viva.a: Carbohydrates provide 4 kcal/gram, proteins provide 4 kcal/gram, and fats provide 9 kcal/gram.

viva.q: What volumes correspond to standard household kitchen measures in dietary recall?
viva.a: One teaspoon is 5 ml, one tablespoon is 15 ml, one standard katori or cup is 150 ml, and one standard glass is 250 ml.

viva.q: Name the three essential fatty acids in human nutrition.
viva.a: The three essential fatty acids are linoleic acid, linolenic acid, and arachidonic acid.
